So much of my heart is in Palestine. And it’s where so much of my energy and attention is focused. She needs that from me (from all of us). 

But what I don’t share much about is how much of my heart is also in South America. 

My Siti, Magdalena, is my best friend. She is my connection to that part of the world. Born & raised in Livramento, Brasil—where my Baba was born—just on the boarder of Rivera, Uruguay. I grew up watching her tailor suits in Baba’s store while stealing sips of her maté 🧉, stirring the pot of feijão so it didn’t burn, getting Vick’s slathered everywhere during a cold, & listening to her & Baba switch between Portuguese & Spanish in a single conversation—something they still do today. 

She is the oldest daughter of a Druze farmer turned photographer named Mahmoud (Maximo in Brasil) who left Lebanon for in Brasil at 16 & never went back, where he met his wife, Dorila, going on to have 6 girls. My great grandparents. 

All 6 girls got married & moved all over the world. Siti almost married a gaucho (cowboy) but when he left for the military, Sidi (who left Palestine for Brasil) swooped in & lovingly stole her away 😏. They eventually moved to the U.S. with my dad & his brother. While one sister married Sidi’s cousin & moved to the States, their other sisters spread throughout South America. To Argentina, Uruguay & Brasil. All of these countries are still home to my family today. And what a blessing that is. 

Migration—a natural part of our existence—has afforded me the beauty of having family to visit all over the world, & of calling so many places “home.” 
While it may be a smaller part of my DNA, being Latina was such a prominent part of my upbringing through Siti. 

I am so unbelievably proud to come from an immigrant Arab Latiné family. And what a beautiful moment & reminder it was yesterday to see some of the flags representing my family as part of the actual “American” line up (🖕🏽 the Super Bowl tho 😅). 

God bless the true America. And may all the nations destroyed, hurt, and overshadowed by U.S. imperialism live forever & always be celebrated & honored.

• Entry via the Libya–Egypt border.
• Safe transit across Egyptian territory with life-saving supplies.
• Full coordination with authorities on security and logistics.
• Direct delivery of food, medicine and winter caravans to Rafah.

Egypt is the gatekeeper. As the only viable artery for relief while the Israeli regime criminalizes aid organizations, Egypt holds a moral, ethical and legal obligation to facilitate this mission. We have no intention to interfere. Our only goal is to reach people who have no other alternative but to survive.

It is time to break the silence and the siege. Stand with us and demand that Egypt open the path for emergency aid.

Here I stand, looking at the one who destroyed my city, stole my childhood and my youth, and burned my dreams before they could grow. I look at the one who killed my father, my relatives, and my friends for no reason, leaving a pain in my chest that never heals. I look at him not out of weakness, but to remind myself that I am still alive, despite everything he tried to kill inside me.

I’m not one to share pictures of food much anymore, especially as it’s being weaponized against my people both back home in Palestine and in the U.S. 

I’ve done my best to abstain from doing so actually, even though it is the antithesis of who we are as a people. As Palestinians, all we do is feed people. All we want to do is feed people. And so much of who we are and our history lives in our cuisine. I love to cook. I love to host. I loved to share videos of me and my kids cooking together once upon another time. But it just doesn’t feel right anymore. 

I’ve shared bits and pieces of my travels over the last few months for book tour (big recap coming soon, maybe), and something I keep gravitating towards sharing from my last weekend in DC was our community’s insistence on keeping that tradition of hosting, and showing love through food, alive throughout my trip - by feeding me and my family. And I want to highlight their spaces and staff and honor and encourage those in or traveling to the DMV area to please visit and support. 

I cannot thank @zandzdc and @albiwashdc enough for taking such incredible care of my family this weekend. From comfort food at Z&Z that felt like being back in the Old City to the intricate flavors in every plate at Albi - a place I’ve been eager to try for years (it has a Michelin star ⭐️!!) that somehow creatively played on our traditional Palestinian dishes while remaining authentic and “so obviously Palestinian.” I got emotional listening to @williamelvin talk about Palestine being the center of the world - “back then” & now. And I got the watch the baby of the Matari-cousin-crew @matari2o in his element at work!

Both places made me feel like they were just as excited to have us, as we were to be there. Their generosity & attention to detail blew me away. And I cannot get over how leaving each kitchen felt like leaving “Tata’s / Siti’s house.” 

I’m so grateful. I will be back. And I hope that all of you go (if you can) and support Palestinian businesses throughout the diaspora. Our food and our people deserve to be celebrated and supported.

A year ago today, my best friend gave birth to the most beautiful Palestinian-Egyptian baby boy and named him Musa. 

After a few weeks in the NICU hoping and praying for good news regarding his lung development, it was confirmed that Musa was born with an incredibly rare lung disease called Alveolar Capillary Dysplasia (ACD). Only about 200 cases worldwide have been formally reported in medical literature since the disease’s initial recognition in 1948. 

The disease has a nearly 100% mortality rate within the first few hours to a few weeks in an infant’s life. By a month in, I was wholly convinced I was about to witness a true medical miracle and that I’d get to see Musa grow up with my boys. Sadly, Musa was only physically with us for one more month, but it is because of him that I still believe in miracles—because his whole short existence was one. 

I watched Musa’s mama—a woman who exuded nothing but joy for the 10+ years I’ve known her—live simultaneously her best and worst days through the last year. She was and still is the best mother to him—and I’ve learned so much from her about what it means to be strong and hopeful for the future. I see the way she honors him every day, and in honor of her, it’s something we try to do with our boys in keeping his memory alive, too. 

Khalto loves you forever habibi Musa 👼🏼. Please continue to watch over your mama and baba and my boys until we can all be reunited one day with you, with the children of Gaza, and all our loved ones (Heaven surely is crowded ❤️‍🩹). I’m so honored I get to carry a piece of you with me always everywhere I go—how special to receive this gift of you on your birthday. 

Happy 1st heavenly birthday to my favorite tiny angel, who happens to be my Sidi’s “resting place” neighbor 🥰. Allah yirhamhom. 

A NOTE: Because of how rare Musa’s disease was, there is not enough research to pinpoint exactly how or why he left us. So in honor of his first birthday, I’d love to raise some funding for ACD research (fundraising sticker attached).

Growing up in Bethlehem, I joined my grandparents on a few olive harvest journeys, and let me tell you—it’s a time like no other. 

I remember the feelings of pride. 

It’s a generational tradition linked to beautiful cultural heritage. “We eat what they [our ancestors] planted. We plant so they [our descendants] eat,” my great aunt would repeat the famous saying.

Beyond the connection to the land and the romance of it all, the season requires serious work. 

Long hours under the sun, picking the fruit, gathering it, carrying it, and hunting down the runaway olives—making sure none goes to waste.

In the end, you receive the blessings of the land: delicious olives and bottles of gold—olive oil.
(Btw, a home-made bottle of olive oil is the best gift you could give someone.)

The olive harvest should be a time of hope. It used to be.

Instead, it’s become a season of fear and control. Israeli settlers attack Palestinian farmers everywhere. International activists who try to help were assaulted, now deported. 
 
But Palestinian farmers keep returning to their groves. Because these trees aren’t just agriculture—they’re ancestry, resistance, and the refusal to disappear.

Our story from the West Bank.

Another olive harvest season in Palestine, another year of displacement for ~7M Palestinians in diaspora. 

2 years ago I discussed a family trip back to Palestine w. my cousin Sarah for our kids to experience the harvest & be immersed in our people’s existence. Having little babies it was difficult to travel— we decided to do annual reunions here until we could all make it back. Our “hafla al zaytoon.” 

3 mo. into planning year 1—the accelerated genocide in Gaza began & we had to beg folks to show up, reminding them that, because colonizers force us to grieve in silence & alone, we needed to get together. To be & move together. 

It was filled w. so much pain & uncertainty of what was to come for our people. We learned Tatreez & rolled grape leaves as our new offerings for year 1. 

Year 2 was up at the farm & was a beautiful reconnection to land. We harvested molokhiya. We learned traditional “ahweeha.” We moved a bit more freely. We talked about how to continuously repay our “diaspora debts” to our homeland and people. 

This year, while we’re all still grieving & learning how to navigate this new world with so many of us missing (especially our children), I saw loved ones moving a bit more joyfully. We went through each other’s clothes like we did when we were kids. We taught the actual kids how to pickle olives. They propagated fig trees & built a taboon oven compliments of Siti Musa (who tuned in on FaceTime from Falasteen). We made shatta w. peppers from the garden. We fed families thanks to the generosity of @ayat.nyc & sent everyone home w. trays of food. We enjoyed fresh knafeh from @nablussweets.nj. And we sang a song about the hopefulness of return becoming a reality. 

Sarah & I talk often about preparing ourselves to be good ancestors. This is how we’ve chosen to do it. I’m hopeful & anxious for the day we get to finally bring this tradition home but for now, what we’ve got going on here is more than alright. And I’m so proud of that (I think the ancestors would be too). 

While this song is not Palestinian, it perfectly captures the essence of our people & I felt the lyrics were perfect for this year’s recap video. Raise hell—until freedom.

On the night of October 8th, at 1 a.m., we received an evacuation order from the Israeli occupation army to leave my hometown of Beit Hanoun. They forced us to flee our town at night, taking nothing with us, mistakenly believing we would return after a few days. We headed to Gaza City, and after a week, we were forced to evacuate to southern Gaza. I had a call with @hannahmoushabeck yesterday to prep for the speech we’re giving this week to a room full of educators on the importance of storytelling and representation in early literature, as it supports refugee children adapting to their new environments away from home. 

Hannah started the call with, “Just FYI we’ve officially sold out of your first print of the book the day before publication day.” 

She also let me know that we’ve raised $7,133 for seed protectors and farmers through our collaboration with @paliheirloomseedlibrary & @canaan.palestine on the special edition boxes. 

And tbh after that I don’t remember much else about the call (which isn’t very good because we have a 45 min speech that we went over after🥲). 

But I just wanted to say, that I’m so grateful. For this community and for your love and support. 

I can’t stress enough how important this project was/is to me. I hope it proves so many things. 

#1 being that—we can make beautiful things happen together. From this entirely Palestinian-woman made book, to the reconfiguration of schedules and venues to make sure our events happen when “they” cancel on us. I am so damn proud of this network we’ve built together. Because it’s a network grounded in the understanding of the importance and validity of Indigenous storytelling—and it’s a network that vows to protect those stories along with the people who tell them. 

I am a product of the displacement that we are watching happen in Gaza and all over Palestine today. It happened to 1/4 of my family in 1948. And I hope if nothing else that this has solidified an understanding that no matter how far we may be from the land and how many generations of us may be missing from Her soil, we will always tell Her and our peoples story. Palestine will never die.

Last week I highlighted this book without telling you anything about it other than the fact that it was completely Palestinian - authored, illustrated, edited, & published.

The truth is I could have done a short & sweet review then, but I wanted to share why I felt especially connected to this story. I just didn’t expect to cry when I sat & wrote it all out.

Everything Grows in Jiddo’s Garden begins with a young girl looking fondly through a photo album with her mama. They talk about their two homes - the one here & one in a land called Palestine. The girl has never been to her ancestral homeland but feels a connection to it through the gifts that grow in her Jiddo’s garden here.

Although the Nakba is a painful part of Palestinian history, I appreciate that this story gently touches on it for even the youngest of readers to empathize with. They can understand it was and still is a difficult memory for those still in Palestine & the diaspora. 

The main character’s conversations with her Jiddo remind me of the conversations I’ve imagined having with my own grandparents. The ones I never got to meet. They experienced the trauma of The Partition where they were separated from their loved ones on the basis of religion & forced to settle in present day Pakistan. Not long after The Partition they relocated to Nigeria for many years where they ultimately passed & where I was eventually born. 

It’s hard to explain how I still feel so connected to their pain even without having heard their stories directly, or even their voices. But the experiences of our families are part of us. This is what we mean when we say it’s all connected - we’re all connected. ❤️

So yeah, this book is some kinda special. 💕

The Donkey. حمار. ḥimār. 

Another connector to the farmers and shepherds of Palestine (and other areas of the Levant and Mediterranean) whose name is commonly used as an insult. Throughout time and across cultures donkeys are often portrayed as stubborn, stupid, and a representative of the “lower class.” 

Even in children’s literature and entertainment, donkeys are the “sad” and “annoying” characters.

And all of this couldn’t be further from the truth.

A lot of folks are new here (on October 7, 2023 I had a platform of 16k, so 351,000 of you to be exact, ha). 

And a lot of people don’t know much about my personal life (now it’s by design, but at one point I was very open in sharing our family). They don’t know that—in addition to being a content creator, producer, writer, storyteller—I’m also a 34 year old wife and mom of 2 boys. 

I had a pretty fresh baby (just turned 1) just before everything (this current genocide) began in Gaza and was just learning how to navigate being a mom of 2 kids while balancing multiple jobs and growing my own company. 

A lot of people asked how I was able to juggle everything especially in the early months of genocide and the truth is - I wasn’t juggling anything at all (I was honest about that when they asked). I had tunnel vision. 

All I could see was what Gaza (and the rest of Palestine) needed and how I could contribute to that from diaspora. I was obsessed with repaying what I call my “diaspora debt” (I still am). So much so that I lost myself a bit for a few months. 

Thankfully, I married a true partner. Someone who knows when I dip below 100%, they go to 120% to fill in the gap. My husband is my rock. He kept it all together when I couldn’t so that I could make sure I was contributing worthy education to make this world better for our kids. And no matter how many times I say “thank you” for filling in during that time and keeping me standing (no matter how wobbly I was), it will never be enough.

Every time I touch this sacred plant (Za’atar) I take a deep breath in and out. A breath filled with so guilt and gratitude, and joy and sadness. 

I get to nurture these leaves (that my grandfather had brought over from someone’s trip to Palestine) and in turn they nourish me and my family - while another Palestinian on our own land where this plant grows naturally and Indigenously - cannot touch it. 

The various parallel lives that we (Palestinians) have all been living, that we ARE all living, is hard to grapple with sometimes. 

I have a hard time reconciling with the fact that the only reason those of us in diaspora are “safe” (relatively) today, is because our grandparents or parents faced what Gaza is facing right now almost 8 decades ago (on a much smaller, less technologically violent and mass weaponry scale). Because multiple generations got to learn to live through the trauma in our bodies that has been reluctantly passed down to each of us no matter how hard we’ve tried to stop it from doing that. Because they survived. And moved around this planet looking for a new home - longing to go back to our true place. 

That’s why I get to be here and touch this plant. Because no matter where both of my grandfathers lived on this earth (and it was many places), they always made sure we knew where “real home” was. 

And I think of how many generations down from the children we’re seeing in Gaza it will take for one of their descendants to have these thoughts and these moments with nature. 

When it shouldn’t have to take “generations” to get there at all.

77 years ago the trajectory of both sides of my family’s lives shifted entirely due to unimaginable, extreme, religious supremacist, colonial violence meant to erase a magnificent people from their land. All of which has been a part of a century-old plan to steal one of our planet’s most mystical and sacred places. 

The Nakba (Arabic for The Catastrophe) was and still is a defining moment in every Palestinian’s life - and it’s something we’re still watching unfold today.

I don’t know of a single Palestinian family that hasn’t been affected by the events of 1948. Whether we survived genocide (like my husband’s family), faced displacement (like my mom’s family), are living under an illegal military occupation and apartheid (like my dad’s and my mom’s family), have had to integrate into the colonizer’s society, or are living under a brutal siege and blockade that has made way for the genocide that we are watching every day today (I often wonder what we’ll call this genocide one day) - every Palestinian moves through this world with the trauma of The Nakba flowing through our veins and coming out in various ways (in writing, music, art, business, our relationships, etc.). 

For me - it’s always been writing. 

I also don’t know of single Palestinian children’s book that doesn’t mention or center The Nakba. Including my own. 

We carry our family stories with us everywhere we go in this world, whether we acknowledge them or not. Whether we speak life to them or not. Whether we are denied of them or not. Whether we choose to honor them or not. 

To every Palestinian in diaspora today - I hope you choose to honor your stories of how you got to where you are today. The ancestors who struggled, who died, who survived, who thrived - so you can be who you are today. 

I hope you choose to honor them. 

One day we will speak of The Nakba as an event of our past. Something that ended with the righteous stewards of the land remaining steadfast and strong until every colonizer has left our soil, and that finally led us to a free Palestine. 

And so it will be. ✨

I grew up not even realizing that my life revolved around storytelling.

I’ve always had a narrator in my head making mental notes, having conversations w. myself to analyze situations. That inner voice never turns off. Literally - never.

I got a degree in journalism & for the longest time I felt like a fraud because it was just so easy. None of it felt hard. I understood everything instinctively: how to tell a story, keep an audience engaged, trigger emotions, what not to say.

I’ve been in PR & media for 14 years. When I started writing publicly in 2015, the media ate it up (#exploitation). Still, I felt like a fraud. 

“How is my writing doing so well?”

“Surely, I can’t write another compelling piece. That was a one-time thing.”

It wasn’t until October 8th, 2023, that I finally understood why my writing “worked.”

Beyond the fancy degree & over a decade in media - I’m just a natural storyteller - like every other Palestinian I know. It’s in our blood.

Coded in our DNA, passed down through generations not just because it made life magical for our ancestors, but because it’s also been a means of survival.

Palestinians are natural-born storytellers. That’s why our journalists have become the international standard for what it means to hold that title w. honor & dignity.

Our power is evident in the way that israel & the U.S. have strategically murdered over 200 of our journalists. In the way that israel & the U.S. have - together - become the single greatest killer of journalists in modern history. In the way that israel & the U.S.’s genocide in Gaza is the deadliest “war” on journalists & media workers *ever to be recorded.* 

That’s how powerful we are. That the world’s most powerful & violent empire (and its little sh*t baby colony) to have ever been in existence is targeting us - & our stories. Our journalism.  

Journalism is not a crime. And we must fight to demand the protection of all journalists - including & especially Palestinian journalists. 

It’s an accepted part of life that our stories will always outlive us - but my God do we deserve to live as long as we possibly can to be able to tell them.

It seems silly to talk about my children’s book when the world is on fire. When our world is on fire. 

And then I remember that projects like this are proof of survival. 

What you’re watching now - was my Jido’s life in 1948 (today, it is on a horrifyingly monstrous scale due to technological advancements). It’s everything he fled from. Genocide. Ethnic cleansing.

In Boston this past weekend we made a point to visit @yafabakerycafe. Before walking in when my 5 year old asked where we were going I told him, “We’re going to a place where everyone loves Palestine.” 

You walk in & are greeted with a sample of their house Chai latte & a mini baklava roll. The owners (two brothers) working behind the counter start a conversation w. everyone who walks in. Ours went like this (as I entered covered in Tatreez & Palestine stickers):

Abdulla: “I like all your Tatreez and stickers! You look more Palestinian than I do.” 

Me: “I would hope so, I’m Palestinian too.” 

It eventually leads to the realization that my great grandmother, Tata Hajja, was from their village of Beit Safafa. 

And then the plates of food & sweets & carafes of mint ginger lemonade just kept coming. Man do we take extra good care of our “village relatives.” 

We show love through food, Palestinians. Which is why it’s especially cruel (as in every case of populations of people being forcefully starved) that this world is adamant on stripping away our access to it. 

That love was evident all throughout this cafe, as I watched Abdulla - in addition to the samples you’re met w. upon entry - hand everyone an ajweh (a date filled sweet) on their way out. It was evident in the way they snuck extra chocolates into our to-go bags for the kids. In the way they topped off our lattes for the long drive back home. 

It was the closest I’ve felt to home in nearly 2 years that I’ve experienced here in the states (this coming from a girl who grew up not far outside of Little Palestine in Paterson). 

In the midst of that conversation w. Abdulla, my son tugged on my sweatpants to get my attention & when I looked down answering him with, “Na’am (yes) Mama?” he asks, “Mama, *everyone* here loves Palestine?” To which I responded teary-eyed with, “Yes Mama. Everyone here loves Palestine.” 

And it was met with the sweetest smile I’ve ever seen on my boy’s face. 🥹🫶🏽

Anyway, if you’re in the Boston area - I highly suggest visiting Yafa Bakery & Cafe. And come August they promised @jiddos.garden would be on display right next to @hannahmoushabeck’s book.🤪🥰

The data, analysis, and stories shared in our new report aim to reflect the vast and severe repression that characterized 2024, but also the resilience that kept Palestinians and allies speaking out despite it, and the many victories that the movement won along the way.

In the colonial world you are taught to view our people and our land the way you view anything that disturbs the idea of perceived “perfection.” (In this sense, it’s anything that doesn’t fit the cookie cutter mold - and anything they simply won’t “obey.”) Similar to the way you view our medicinal plants as “weeds being unruly to your plans of perfect grass.

This world despises Indigeneity - so much that it spends trillions on doing everything it can to kill it. To kill us. Poisoning you along the way. 

This world despises us - because things that “just won’t die” are a nuisance to your plans of colonization. Just like the “weeds” you try to remove - we are persistent. 

Indigeneity always persists.

To the ones who know this place can be better for our kids.

As we watch our education system be pummeled into the ground (that they’re also destroying with bombs & poison), we have to fill in the gaps that have always existed & will only get bigger the longer they’re ignored.

We have to recognize the part we (can) play in the lives of the children in our communities—something my mother taught me early on.

Every year in elementary school, she came in with sweets, Arabi string cheese, bread, Labneh, thobes, keffiyehs, books—teaching my classmates about their (for a long time, only) Arab & Muslim friend. I loved it, but I was anxious.

“Will they like the food?”
 “Will they think our outfits are weird?”
 “Will they mock our language & music?”

No matter how well it was received, it never became part of the curriculum (a bit different now, but DEI is being rolled back).

Teaching about Palestine & Islam in schools became something I saw as my job before I even had kids. A responsibility to the community & to kids like me—to make them feel seen & proud. To remind teachers & administrators that their students come from different cultures & to be conscious of that.

I’ve taught kids from kindergarten to high school, in person & virtual, teaching them to love who we are through food, music, dance, & fashion.

And this year, I finally got to do it for my own kid. 🥹

The rules are different now—no food, so we do crafts 🙂— but I watched as nothing but joy & pride existed on my kid’s face as he wore his disdasha & hatta, shared about Ramadan & Eid, & listened to Arabi music while making Eid crafts w. his friends. 

He was everyone’s best friend that day after passing out Eid goodie bags. 🙊

What I’ve learned: Teachers are overburdened & underappreciated, and they welcome our help. They will invite you in if you ask. And they will be so, so kind.

If we want to be seen & heard, if we want to make a difference, we need to make room for ourselves in these spaces. This place won’t do it for us—we show them how it’s done. 9.9/10 times, it’s well received & moves the needle in the right direction, but we have to do our part.

(bless my mama. Alhamdullilah for this lesson.)

We added another ancestor to the corner yesterday. 

My 3amo Osama. Jido’s youngest brother. 

Born in Ein Karem, Palestine in 1947 - he was a just-months-old baby being carried into displacement and eventually exile during the Nakba. Like the same just-months-old babies we’re watching being violently thrust into the same scenario today in Gaza. 

He was my mama’s “fun uncle.” And he was that for me and my brothers too when we’d visit overseas. 

One of my strongest memories of him was when he picked us up from the airport - I was about 11 or 12 years old - and we sat in the front seat of his sedan, the front seat was more like a long couch cushion (what are seatbelts lol), and he took us to the pet store upon arrival and got me and my brothers two love birds — a yellow and a blue one — because he wanted to make sure we had pets to play with during our trip. 

Something he used to do for my mom when she’d spend summers with him as a kid (for her it was a baby lamb every year that she eventually realized they’d be eating at the end of every summer vacation but - that’s another story for another day 🥲). 

It was a privilege to have had the time with him that we did. And even more of a privilege to take a trip back to visit him after I got married so he could meet my husband, and then a few years later with our two children. 

Our elders are leaving us before we have the chance to take them back home. Something that reminds me every day of how important it is to fight for the right of return for those who are still with us and in the honor of those we’ve lost along the (very long, very difficult) way. 

Allah yirhamhak ya 3amo. Thank you for the beautiful memories. I promise to talk of you always with my children.

Between October 2023 and September 2024, Israeli authorities’ actions have deprived the majority of the more than 2 million Palestinians living in Gaza of access to even that bare minimum amount of water, which has contributed to death and widespread disease. For many in Gaza, much or all of the water they have had access to is not suitable for drinking.

“If we can’t find drinkable water, we drink the sea water,” one father displaced to a school in Rafah told Human Rights Watch in December 2023. “It happened to me many times when I had to drink the sea water. You don’t understand how much we are suffering.”

Israel’s destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system, including its ability to track diseases, has made it impossible to fully understand the true scale of harm and deaths caused by the deprivation of adequate water. The full extent may never be known.

However, these policies have likely resulted in thousands of deaths.
Doctors and nurses told Human Rights Watch they have witnessed numerous infants, children, and adults die from a combination of malnutrition, dehydration, and disease.

The intent to cut off essential services was explicitly stated by Israeli officials in October 2023 and has been reflected in the actions of occupation forces since.

Israel continues to violate the provisional ICJ measures to prevent genocide, including “the deprivation of access to adequate food and water.”

Human Rights Watch recommends international states take measures to prevent further atrocities, including “targeted sanctions, suspension of arms transfers and military assistance, and review of bilateral trade and political agreements, to put concrete pressure on the Israeli government to comply with the ICJ’s provisional measures and its other obligations under IHL and human rights law.”

My children (yes they are really 5 and 2 and yes we *really* have these conversations and yes they *really* understand) have done a lot of growing in the past 14 months. They’ve learned things I hadn’t intended on teaching them until they were a bit older. 

You always try to shield your children from pain and fear but kids in Palestine don’t have that privilege. And my children are Palestinian so having these conversations about their brothers and sisters and cousins back home is the absolute bare minimum of what I can do as a Palestinian mom in diaspora. 

They’ve noticed we’ve lost “friends” and that our lifestyle has changed a bit - and also that they think a bit differently than their peers. And I’ve learned to embrace that and see some beauty in it. 

My children speak of the earth she’s a relative we care for (because she is). They feel sadness when they find an insect or animal that has reached its lifespan (we gave a bumble an honorable burial in our garden this spring 🥺 🐝). They ask when we’re moving to Palestine excitedly and talk about our house there often. They ask to see pictures of back home and about all the things we’ll do when we return (like build a farm with a big garden, one horse, and “so many goats” [? I try not to question them too much 🙂]). 

They’re smart. Children are smart. And they’re capable of understanding this world as well as lending their own perspectives on things. 

I’m so proud of them. And I’m so proud to be their mom. 

Please teach your kids about us (and all Indigenous folks). Raise them with awareness and empathy. It’s never too early to start. The world will be better for it. 🇵🇸

These camps are now under threat not only from airstrikes but also from the relentless winter weather.

Louise Wateridge, spokesperson for the UN’s Palestinian refugee agency (UNRWA), warns that winter rains could flood lower-lying areas with sewage, threatening half a million people in Gaza.

“When it rains, sewage is going to pile up in lower [elevation] areas. All displaced people are using makeshift toilets, trying to keep sewage away from their shelters, but it ends up accumulating elsewhere, often in streets or near others’ shelters. Malnourished people will get sicker because it all works together against their health and wellbeing,” Wateridge said.

Since I was little I remember fearing death. 

Less in the sense that I was afraid of dying myself, and more that I was afraid of everyone I loved around me dying first. It had been a focal point of my anxiety and one of my (many lol) reasons for so many years in therapy. It wasn’t until my cousin (who - surprise - is also a therapist) had asked me why I was “prematurely mourning (my) living loved ones” that I realized I was even doing that. 

Fear of others dying is still something I mentally wrestle with every day but over the last few years (and especially during this last year) I’ve learned that rather than fearing death, I can find ways to honor it and respect it instead. Something I haven’t been able to find connection with through Islamic teaching (yet) but that I’ve been learning more from and always admired about Día de los Muertos celebrations. 

Though I’ve never arranged one myself, I developed a deep affection for ofrendas and they have made death “less scary” for me. A “celebration” my cousins and I had been planning long before 10/7/23, where the first year (which was at my house) was instead turned into a weekend of grieving more than it was celebrating as it fell roughly two weeks into the current genocide in Gaza. It was meant to be a weekend where we all reunited (flying in from wherever we are to wherever it takes place that year) and honored the annual olive harvest in Palestine that none of us have been a part of but plan on taking part in one day soon (something Palestinians are murdered for and while doing). An act of love and resistance that is engrained in our peoples’ DNA. 

This year it took place up north at my cousin’s farm where we truly lived off the land for the weekend. 

There was a bit more joy than last year as we’re all learning how to forever coexist with grief and joy and pride the way our ancestors have for at least the last 100 years. We sat around the fire and drank endless pots of shai. We played with the animals. We made ikras and harvested mlokhiya together. We learned to zaghrat and “aweeha.” We moved our bodies and lounged in thobes. 

We laughed. We cried. We cursed this world for taking so much from us and we brought each other back to a place of softness and gratitude for all that we still have and all that we’ve managed to protect and preserve in the global effort to erase us from existence over the last century. 

We just existed. As our whole selves in whatever part of our self identification journey each of us was in, we just existed - as Palestinians. 

We need these moments of just being. If we’re going to survive this as a people, and come out of us with our traditions intact - we need these moments. 

Please do not demand anything of us. Please do not tell us how to grieve. Please do not tell us how to move in this world. Please just let us exist. (And this isn’t a request - this is a demand.)

Indigenous Protects Indigenous. 

A story about my “Native auntie” Noelle who has taught me so much the last 10 years of what it means to hold Indigeneity & sit in that power. 

She’s a grounding forces & has taught me more about my garden, plant medicine, how to stay mentally strong in this fight, & about what I’m capable of as an Indigenous woman. My source when I need to confirm my mind is taking me down the right path. That “Indigenous instinct check.” 

I’ve also over the years learned more about her people (note: she is Apache of Geronimo’s tribe & that power 😮‍💨) & how to show up better I’m needed (I still must be better here but she affords us so much grace given the times). 

I believe in sharing our cultures but *only when we offer pieces of it to each other*. She texted me randomly one day that she sent me ghost beads because she “just felt like (I) you needed some extra protection,” along with some readings about them. 

I’ve learned that ghost beads are actually dried juniper berries collected after ants have found the berries on the ground & nibbled off one end & eaten the inside of the berry until they’re hollowed & dry. 

They’re meant to represent interconnection with the earth, animals & humans & they’re worn to bring about peace, harmony & safety. She told me to hang it next to my bed to help keep away the bad dreams to which I responded, “I don’t remember the last time I had a bad dream now that I think about it, how odd?” To which she replied, “You have been too busy facing them during the day.” 

In that moment it was a nice reminder that someone recognized my pain wholly, & that they were living proof that there is life “after” it to look forward to - or at least a life where the pain coexists “neatly” with the joy. 

Indigenous people are in so much pain. We recognize ourselves in one another’s struggles & we get wiser & stronger the more connected we all become. 

We have so much to learn from each other. 

May we all always find each other in every lifetime. To strategize & fight & just “be.” The world is so much better when we lead & I’m looking forward to the day we can return to that order.

Collective punishment during war refers to the punitive measures taken by a military or occupying force against a group of people in response to the actions of a few individuals, typically as retaliation for resistance or acts of defiance. These actions target civilians or a larger community rather than specific perpetrators, violating international laws and human rights.

Key examples of collective punishment include:
1. **Blockades and sieges**: Preventing access to essential goods like food, water, and medical supplies for entire communities.
2. **Destruction of property**: Systematically destroying homes, infrastructure, or livelihoods in response to an attack or resistance.
3. **Mass arrests or detentions**: Detaining large numbers of civilians to pressure a resistance group.
4. **Curfews and travel restrictions**: Imposing severe movement restrictions on entire populations.
 
Under international law, particularly the **Geneva Conventions**, collective punishment is prohibited. It is considered a violation of human rights and the laws of war because it punishes innocent civilians for actions they did not commit.

Na3na. 

Mint. 

I grew up with a backyard full of mint. It went in everything mama and my grandmothers cooked. Salad. Dressings. Marinades. Tea. 

When I was a little girl Siti and Sidi (Allah yirhamho Sidi - I miss him) would come over on Thursdays so mama could work, and we would lay in the backyard with cut fruit and Siti would pick off na3na leaves for us and we would just sit in the grass and chew on the leaves. 

Such a tiny but mighty plant - literally cannot get rid of it - and such an integral part of our culture. 

This is a cutting from a mint stem my husband’s grandfather (Allah yirhamho) brought to the States from Jerusalem in the 1980s.  It’s a bit different than other mint we’ve grown here. Very flat, smooth, thin leaves with a small amount of veining compared to the usual coarser, thicker and rougher leaves I’ve usually dealt with - almost like you can tell it’s old 🙂. 

He planted it in his backyard in New Jersey and since then it’s been making its rounds to different family members’ homes, one stem at a time. My mother in law gave me a stem - no roots - and I kept it alive and helped it grow. 

A piece of home that has survived off of its ancestral land for more than 3 decades, with those of us displaced from our homes for even longer caring for it and keeping it going. 

Just like the na3na plant, they cannot get rid of us. Ever. 

I’m looking forward to the day when we return, where I’ll get to also return this na3na plant to its original soil.

The Six-Day War was a conflict between Israel and several Arab states, including Egypt, Jordan, and Syria. The war began on June 5, 1967, and ended on June 10, lasting just six days, hence its name.

During the war, Israel launched a preemptive strike against Egypt’s air force, quickly gaining air superiority. Israeli forces then advanced into the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza Strip, West Bank, and Golan Heights, capturing these territories from Egypt, Jordan, and Syria.

One of the most significant outcomes of the war was Israel’s occupation of East Jerusalem, including the Old City and its holy sites such as the Western Wall and Al-Aqsa Mosque. This occupation remains a contentious issue in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to this day.

The war also resulted in a massive influx of Palestinian refugees and further territorial disputes, setting the stage for decades of conflict and geopolitical tensions in the region.

A bit of motherly advice - if I may - for my fellow Muslims on the internet this month (particularly those in the food content creation space but not limited to the professionals). Gaza is always watching. Let’s be mindful these next 30 days.

Today was our very last day of cooking for displaced families in my neighborhood in Rafah city. Over the past 4 months, my family and I were able to cook and distribute food for at least 75 families a day, 4 times a week.

It started with my family and me using our own pocket money and even our clothes to help our new neighbors and guests. Then, my wholesome little community, followers and online friends decided to take action instead of spectating us! 

At first, those guests were coming from the north of Gaza, leaving everything behind and escaping the death toll, followed by people from Khan Younis.

I cooked for those people with a serious knee injury, without access to therapy, medications, or painkillers, even until I couldn't anymore. Through donations, I was not only able to finance 4 days of cooking weekly but also to use the remaining funds to get aid for governmental schools that had displaced families in them while the UN refused to help(which was something i have never mentioned before actually)

I have refused to show myself or my people's struggle, i refused to use any of this as content even tho i had the chance to!

I have also provided enough proof for my community to trust and keep supporting us at the same time by either posting on stories or showing whoever asks for proof in the DMS enough proof to convince them.

I have been suffering a lot mentally and physically without any access to therapy, physical therapy, or medications, with or without war. I lost so many dear people and friends, more than 270 relatives since the beginning of this genocide, and my one wish is to evacuate myself and my family to Egypt for an urgent knee surgery while my family accompanies me.

7 hours. 

That was all I got with my motherland for the first time in 18 years. 

We weren’t even supposed to go. We didn’t want to go for such a short amount of time because we knew it’d never be enough. But we did it anyway. 

Took a chance, crossed the border from Jordan, got in and spent the day in the Old City and felt “home” and grounded for the first time in my almost 33 years in this life. 

7 hours with the land. 

2 hours with my cousin in Al Quds whom I hadn’t seen in almost 2 decades. 

~35 minutes with his mom and sister Amena (my cousin whom you’ve all grown to love) who *just happened to be there visiting from Gaza that day*. 

~15 minutes with my best friend who moved to Palestine and *just happened to go into labor 2 weeks early that morning and had a baby* whom I got to meet along with her husband for the first time when I surprised her in the hospital on my way back to get through the border before it closed for the day. 

Zero time with my other cousins throughout Occupied Palestine (the West Bank) because they couldn’t get visas approved to meet us in Al Quds for lunch. 

So much happened in those 7 hours that still blows my mind knowing almost exactly 2 months later I’d watch my homeland and people being desecrated more violently than usual for 137 days straight. 

I kept wondering if that trip happened because God/the Universe was giving me an opportunity to say “goodbye” to Palestine or if it was because I needed a reminder of what to fight for because of what was to come. The thought of that being the “last time” absolutely ripped my heart out every day for almost a month when the genocide in Gaza first started. 

I’ve now realized it’s a bit of both. 

I *was* saying goodbye to Palestine. 

The occupied one. 

The apartheid-controlled one. 

The blood-soaked one. 

Because the next time I’ll be back (which will be much sooner than 18 years from now), it will be a different Palestine. 

A liberated one - from every inch between the river and the sea (something I truly, intuitively believe I will see). 🇵🇸

The signature lira headpieces from Lira Co. Jewelry are inspired by the Palestinian Shatwa- a head covering adorned with coins typically worn by married women. All proceeds from headbands sales will be donated to the Palestinian Children’s Relief Fund. 

“An abundance of coins worn on headdresses, like the shatweh, saffeh and the wuqayet darahim, but also on simpler bonnets, showed the geographical range of economic contacts. Since 1948, Palestinian jewellery has moved with refugees to Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and further abroad. Much of it was sold to cover survival needs or passage to a safer place, and as such the heritage jewellery of Palestine is less widely known than other forms of traditional jewellery from Southwest Asia. Tiraz Centre in Amman, as well as museums all over the world, work tirelessly to keep the connection of this jewellery to its geographical and cultural origins alive.
Tell el-Ajjul, the location of ancient Gaza and near the modern town, was a place where gold jewellery was produced in the late Bronze Age.”

When 9/11 is taught in schools, it is missing a massive portion of necessary education for our children to understand this. That missing piece is the rise in Islamophobia. 

Hate crimes against Muslims increased at an alarming rate. So many young Americans rushed to enlist in the military to “avenge” 9/11 in hopes of being deployed to countries that had nothing to do with those attacks, simply because they were Muslim majority. 

Islamophobia is just as much an important piece of this country’s 9/11 history as the attacks themselves. And teachers (and parents) today have a responsibility to ensure that our children are equipped with that knowledge. 

Remembering those 2,977 Americans we lost 22 years ago today. Those who thought it was a normal day at work or of travel. Those who so bravely ran into the wreckage to save another life & in turn lost their own. 

May we also remember the brief moment of unity we had as we collectively grieved our neighbors & worked to pick up the pieces of our nation’s shattered heart.

“Zawiya Boukharia” 

Located on Via Dolorosa, the road that holds the handprint of prophet Jesus after he paused to rest while carrying the cross on his back to his own crucifixion, there remains a part of my maternal family’s history - The Boukhari Family. 

While my Jido is 100% indigenous Palestinian, my Taita’s family arrived to Palestine in the 1600s from Bukhara, Uzbekistan to spread the teachings of Sufi Islam. Every one of us with Boukhari blood has some type of mystical intuition flowing through our veins and it’s become something I’ve learned to rely on and trust as I get older and “find myself”. It’s a blessed, special, and ancient connection with God that can’t really be described in written or spoken word. 

I see these double turquoise doors in my dreams. They are the entrance to my “safe space” when I am wrestling with my anxiety. And the arches of our family home in Palestine are much more calming than the rigidity of the structures typically built in the States. So much so that I find myself trying to recreate this place in my home in America. 

Once crossing through the doors you find artifacts of my family’s history in every room. From the traditional Uzbek dresses to the trinkets in protective glass cases that each tell a story - my great great grandfather, Sheikh Yacoub Boukhari - turned it into a space where Sufi leaders from all over the world would visit to experience the magic of Jerusalem. 

I cannot accurately express how much gratitude I have for my aunt and cousins who work tirelessly to protect and maintain their home for our whole family. It’s survived occupation after occupation from the Ottoman’s to the British to now Israeli - it will continue to survive and hold our family’s stories - inshallah 🤲🏽❤️ 🧿

It’s been 18 years since my cousin and I last saw each other. 

This photo is from the rooftop of our family home in the Old City in Jerusalem, on Via Dolorosa, the road where Jesus paused to rest as he carried the cross to his own crucification. 

Izzo (to me, “Iz” to everyone else) and his family have worked over the years to preserve our family history in that home - which has essentially become a museum of the Sufi legacy our family brought to Palestine - where they also offer cooking classes to teach family recipes like the famous “Rooz Boukhari”. 

Sometime in the last 18 years Izzo became the unofficial mayor of the Old City. There wasn’t a street we walked down together or a shop that we walked into where he didn’t know the owner who he’d then insist take care of us making it known that we were family who belonged here - not tourists. It gave me a glimpse of what it could’ve been like if our part of the family hadn’t been displaced all those years ago. 

Over the years I’ve really struggled with my identity and have been searching for that feeling of “belonging” to the point where I feel pains in my chest. But those 7 hours in Jerusalem reminded me that there is a place in this world where I 100% belong. I felt my ancestors presence throughout every inch of the city. And it’s a feeling that I will be desperately grasping on to and carrying with me everywhere until I return. 

Palestine is my home. 

If you ever find yourself in the Old City - please support Izzo and sign up for one of his incredible food tours through his platform @sacredcuisine !! Visitors from all over the world fly in just to experience his tour. 

Family should never be separated - but I’m grateful to live in a time where it’s a little easier to feel closer together no matter how far apart you may be.

PALESTINE 101: Storytelling Through Tatreez

Welcome back to class! 

Today we’ll be learning from Lina Barkawi of @linasthobe about the history behind storytelling through embroidery - or “Tatreez” - that was once present throughout a Palestinian woman’s dress/thobe. 

Based on the colors and motifs used, the Tatreez on a thobe could tell you everything from that woman’s relationship status, to her financial and social status, to her health condition, and the village she’s from, etc. 

After our displacement in 1948, Tatreez became a way for Palestinian refugee women to generate sources of income (more on that from Sara at @deerah.co next week!) while also grasping onto the tradition and its connection to Palestine. In the early days of the 1st intifada, women sewed the colors of the Palestinian flag into their dresses in response to Israeli confiscation of Palestinian flags. It was a way to showcase Palestinian pride and defy and push back on our occupiers. 

Tatreez experiencing its own revolution as Palestinians throughout the diaspora work to reclaim this part of our heritage and bring the practice back to its roots of storytelling. 

Lina has opened up a creative way to do that through her “Lina’s Thobe” business where, after a consultation call, she’ll work with you to design a fully custom thobe from fit, to colors, to motifs, that will tell the story of you and your ancestry just like our thobes once did for the Palestinian women of our past ❤️🇵🇸 

Be sure to follow her page to learn more and keep up with her work! And stay tuned for some more classes on Tatreez from other incredible creators in the space to come 🙏🏽

The keffiyeh is a staple of Palestinian resistance. 

Popularized as a form of protest during the British Occupation of Palestine, it was worn during the Arab Revolt in 1936, by Palestinian freedom fighters to hide their identity and avoid arrest as they revolted against the British Mandate. When the British banned the keffiyeh, many members of the community started wearing it to make it harder for the British to identify those who rebelled against them, cementing its status in the resistance, solidified during the 1st and 2nd intifadas. 

Today it is no less important, as the keffiyeh is viewed as a symbol of identity for us Palestinians. ✊🏽❤️🇵🇸

You know your body best. 

Repeat: you know your body best. 

I was pretty open about how difficult this last pregnancy was for me. 

My OBGYN practice just kept reiterating how “easy” of a patient I was for them because I was one of the few “pregnant women these days” who wasn’t high risk (they literally said this to me every appointment). I didn’t see a doctor for more than 7 min at a check up all 10 months. 

Whenever I told them I was in debilitating pain they told me it was normal and just an unfortunate reality of pregnancy. Something I refused to believe because I felt wonderful while carrying Asad. I took it upon myself to find a pelvic floor specialist and acupuncturist to try and get some relief. 

But the last 3 weeks of being pregnant something felt REALLY off. More pain than usual. I had gained 10 lbs then lost 5 then gained 10 again in between my WEEKLY apts when my diet didn’t change and I was moving even more. All things I tried to express concern with that the doctors brushed off - and all signs of #preeclampsia that went ignored. One doctor literally said “cool it with the food” when I asked about my weight. 

It wasn’t until I told them I was seeing stars that they took it seriously (and even then I had to insist to be seen when the nurse on the phone said “sometimes that happens when you move too quickly” and I responded with “I was laying in bed watching tv…”). 

My blood pressure was rising and the protein levels in my urine were increasing with every visit (I had no idea until they were reviewing my records in the hospital) and no one thought to pay attention to it until I advocated for myself and insisted on being seen because I knew the signs (and that was only because my mother had preeclampsia when pregnant with me). 

Hospital tests confirmed I had preeclampsia, and Yahya was safely delivered 8 hours after an unplanned induction. 🙏🏽 

All this to say - Women’s health care is trash (even with all female medical professionals) and you MUST be your own advocate. It is essential to your life and wellbeing.

PART 1: Today marks the 74th year of commemorating “Al Nakba”. 

In Arabic, “Al Nakba” means “catastrophe”, which accurately describes the mass displacement and ethnic cleansing of indigenous Palestinians from Palestine. 

Many people mark the start year of Al Nakba as 1948 because that was the official beginning of the state of Israel causing a mass exodus of our people to happen, but plans of the theft of Palestine were in motion years prior (like, 1882 prior). The major events that catapulted us into Al Nakba were as follows: 

1️⃣ (1882) “The First Aliyah”: The first official Zionist settlement erects in Palestine founded by Edmond James de Rothschild. 

2️⃣ (1896) Theodor Herzl publishes his “The Jewish State” pamphlet detailing his plans for a an independent Jewish state as a response to global antisemitism, in which Argentina was also being strongly considered as the place for the creation of Israel, not just Palestine. 

3️⃣ (1901) Creation of The Jewish National Fund (JNF): Created solely for obtain land in historic Palestine for Jewish settlements - later having a strong hand in the removal of Palestinians from Palestine. 

4️⃣ (1917) Balfour Declaration: Thanks to the pressures of rising Zionism, this was a letter in support of the idea of a Jewish State in Palestine written by Arthur Balfour to the Rothschild dynasty.  Essentially the “green light” for the creation of Israel. 

5️⃣ (1917) WWI ends and the British Mandate of Palestine begins. 

6️⃣ (1935 - 1947) Jewish terrorist militias formerly known as the Irgun, the Stern, and the Haganah (who were responsible for the massacre of Deir Yassin) are formed. Today, you know those militia groups as the Israeli Defense Force (IDF). 

7️⃣ (1947) the UN passes Resolution 181 partitioning Palestine, giving 54% of the already occupied land to Jewish settlers who at the time owned 7% of the land, and who had lived there for less than 10 years.

Atayef is one of those desserts that just screams “Ramadan” and I was determined to make it work for my dietary needs. This is my Khalti Haya’s recipe! It’s all literally cup for cup replacement to go from glutinous fluffy pancake to #glutenfree *almost just as good 🫠* (let’s be honest it will never be the real thing and I’ve accepted that) pancakes. 

PANCAKE INGREDIENTS:
🔸2 cups fine ground corn meal (replacement for semolina) 
🔸1 cup all purpose GF flour (my favorite is @bobsredmill) 
🔸1 tsp sugar 
🔸1 tsp yeast 
🔸1.5 tsp baking powder 
🔸Pinch of salt 
🔸2.5-3 cups of lukewarm water (add or reduce as needed) 

Add all the ingredients in the blender and blend until well combined. You should have a similar consistency to pancake batter! 

Let it sit for 20-30 min (this is super important when GF as the longer it sits the better it rises and bubbles when cooking - I’ve even left the batter to sit overnight!). 

Use a griddle over low-med heat and use ¼ measuring cup to pour onto your griddle. Cook until the center is full of “holes” and dry! Don’t flip it! You’re only cooking one side. 

FILLING INGREDIENTS (non traditional):

MAQLOUBA 🇵🇸 

The absolute ultimate Palestinian comfort dish (and arguably the National dish of Palestine), “maqlouba” translates to “upside down” which is exactly how this dish is made! 

I always thought this was so much more complicated than it actually is. It definitely takes a bit of time but with some adjustments (I.e. baking the veggies instead of frying) you can cut down prep and cook time significantly and multitask in between. 

I’m on a mission to write down my family’s most cherished recipes (including some of my own like the below) for you all to enjoy because food = love to the Palestinian heart & soul and I love you all! 

LOOSE RECIPE (remember I hardly measure anything so it’s all eyeballed like the aspiring Tata that I am 😇)

INGREDIENTS:
🍗 chicken thighs (prefer this cut over any other because they are less likely to dry out when cooking) 
🧄 garlic (1 tbsp)
🧅 onion (1 diced) 
🥔 potatoes (2 peeled and sliced into thin rounds)
🍆 eggplant (1 sliced into thin rounds)
🥕 carrots (about 6 or 7 large carrots peeled, cut into halves/quarters and sliced in halves) 
🌸 cauliflower (1/2 head cut into pieces) 
🍚 rice (3 cups) 

SPICES: 
Cook with chicken, onions, and garlic in extra virgin olive oil
⚫️ 7 spice (2 tbsp)
⚫️ cumin (1 tbsp)
⚫️ all spice (1 tbsp)
⚫️ salt (1 tbsp)
⚫️ black pepper (1 tbsp)

Add a sprinkle onto the sliced veggies and baked on 400° for 30 minutes. And then about 1 tsp of each (minus the salt) into 4.5 cups of boiling water along with one chicken bouillon cube to be poured over the pot once rice is added. 

Bring to a boil and cook on simmer for about 45 min - 1 hr. 

Flip. Reveal. And enjoy 🤤

The Welsh word for a level of “nostalgia” and homesickness that is indescribably heartbreaking but a feeling that is welcomed by many who have lost something they never actually had the chance to experience.

We find solace within one another. We have shared experiences and shared traumas that make us appreciate our time and connection together be it in real life or through the Internet. Through our food, clothes, music, art, etc. A Palestinian living in exile in the U.S. shares a special bond with a Palestinian living in Germany, etc. that cannot be replicated through even decades of friendships with someone of any other identity. Sure, it’s a trauma bond, but it’s one that can be beautiful.

The pressure finally made me explode, and after weeks of crying to my therapist & her giving me permission to give MYSELF permission to take care of me for a while (#boundaries), dare I say I feel a bit - lost - without my focus being on that role? 

To my fellow “older sisters” & “eldest daughters”, these are YOUR words. Thank you for being vulnerable with me & helping me with this one. This is me, giving YOU (mama ❤️) permission to give yourself a break.

I am so emotional today with all of the videos I’ve seen of international soccer players holding up our flag 🇵🇸and other Arabs belting our national anthem with so much pride. Our sh*tty Arab leaders may have forgotten us but our collective people never will 🙏🏽❤️ and I can’t help but cry every time I’m reminded of that. 

I started this social media journey back in May and I’m not sure all of you understand what’s at risk for Palestinians who are outspoken in media and online. This isn’t just a fun experience for me that I stumbled into where I share beautiful thobes and photos of my family to pass the time. It was a calculated decision to curate a new way of educating others en masse and defying our occupiers in a way that would garner unquestionable empathy and solidarity with my people - if you’re human. 

You simply cannot learn from my page and my stories, without it unraveling the Israeli narrative that we never existed, that we do not exist now, and that we are not oppressed. 

The first and last time I was in Palestine was in 2005. And I’m not sure I’ll be able to get back in any time soon for as long as we’re under Israeli occupation. 

Part of the danger of being outspoken about my Palestinian heritage and speaking out against the occupation (in addition to potentially losing your job and/or being kicked out of school) is that, for as hard as it is already for Palestinians living quietly throughout the diaspora to return home - it is nearly impossible for those of us who open our mouths to be granted entry. Meaning there’s a solid chance that I’ve willingly “given up” (had it stolen from me) my ability to see my family in Palestine, to make sure the world knows and understands what is happening to us. 

If there’s any silver lining to that reality - it’s that you’ve all proven to me that none of it has been in vain. 

I’ll leave you with something said in my most recent conversation with my Jido, who is a 1948 refugee from Ein Karem. After asking him, “Do you think we’ll ever get Ein Karem back?” He responded with, “Even if we get just half of it - or if they’d at least allow us to just visit, that would be nice.” 

We all just want to be “home.”

6 years ago I went on a first date with a man who I unknowingly crossed paths with multiple times over the last (at the time) 24 years of my life. 

It was a breakfast date at a diner in Hoboken called “Turning Point” (which I later learned is “bold” for a first date setting). Quite poetic looking back on it as that morning was truly a turning point in my life. 

I was late due to traffic but I got there first, which never happens. He was stuck in traffic too. We later learned that all of Hoboken was experiencing flooding due to a pipe bursting, and Turning Point was actually one of the only places open that morning (as it sits towards the end of the city line). 

I patiently sat at the front, twitching as I always do when I’m nervous, and when I saw him walk in the butterflies I was feeling suddenly calmed. 

I ordered a full dish and 2 sides off the menu and ate it all. Something I had never done on dates prior but I felt so comfortable being myself, I cracked a joke along the lines of, “I could order a small salad and lie to you but figuring I’d show you how I really eat day 1”. 

We spent 2 magical, normal, comforting, sweet and laughter-filled hours together. 

I drove him to his car after. Got out and hugged him. And the moment I got back in and closed the door I called my best friend and told her I had met the man I was going to marry. 

People talk about love with so much ✨drama✨. And while it can be quite dramatic at times, meeting “your person” is the total opposite. I had always had trust & jealousy issues and wondered how I’d ever trust someone enough to marry and feel secure. Something I saw as a fault in myself was really just my intuition telling me “this ain’t it, fam.” 

From the moment I met Saif, I felt… safe (lucky me I get to crack that joke the rest of my life 😆). No insecurities. No questioning. No wondering what he was thinking or doing. It was the proverbial butterflies and fireworks, but with an overwhelming sense of serenity and comfort. And that’s how I knew. 

I count my blessings daily, and thank God & the Universe always for finally allowing us to meet while our paths were once again crossing. 🧿#alhamdulillah

This is my Sidi (grandfather) - known as Sidi Sheikh to everyone else. 

Mustafa Ismail Matari. When I speak of my “ancestors” giving me the strength to share our family’s stories - it’s often him who I feel the strongest connection to - a connection that only grew deeper after his passing. 

He was a FORCE, let me tell you. No one messed with Sidi. He was born and raised in Beit Anan, Palestine (our family is still there). He had a 4th grade education, and was one of the smartest people you’d ever meet. He spoke 4 languages (but only used 3 because he refused to speak English - “the colonizers language” to him), owned his own businesses, opened up a mosque for our community (before “Sidi’s mosque” opened I’m told Muslims in his area used to pray in an Armenian church), spoke in true Falah 3arabi (“ch” sounds and all!), he took care of everyone here and everyone “back home”, and he had unwavering faith like I’ve never seen before. 

Sidi’s journey to American citizenship involved a bit of a “happy accident” - that resulted in my literal existence. 

After deciding he wanted to leave Palestine to find more opportunity in the U.S., Sidi got on a boat that said “America” not realizing that there was both a North and South. When he landed in Brasil, he met my beautiful Brasilian grandmother, Magdalena (whom he called Amina), and had my dad and his brother. 

I’m rusty on the details after that, but Sidi finally landed in New York on October 12th 1964. Because rarely did anyone in his generation actually know their birth date, he chose the next day, October 13th, as his birthday - and his gift to himself was a new life of opportunity for him and his family - my family - in the place he’d always dreamed of getting to. 

Today would have been his 97th birthday. I know he’d be so proud of all of us, and I know he’d be hopeful about the state of his beloved #Falasteen seeing our generations dedication to freedom and the way we’ve moved forward in strength and unity these past few months to reclaim our narrative. 

Allah yirhamhak Sidi, we miss you so much ❤️ happy heavenly birthday 🎈#myPalestinianSidi

Za’atar, such a varying complex blend of spices. Depending on what region of the Middle East you’re from, or even as specific as what city, your Za’atar will look and taste slightly different. 

One thing is for certain, no matter the complexity of the blend you prefer or the difference in spices within the mixture, whenever an Arab eats Za’atar, it’s always the same result. Simply put - it tastes like home. 

Typically a blend of dried oregano, thyme, and/or marjoram, with sumac and toasted sesame seeds, Za’atar can be used in so many ways from meat rubs and marinades to salad topics and garnishes. 

I grew up in a humble home, where Za’atar was always eaten by drenching a piece of Arabi (pita) bread into fresh #Palestinian olive oil, and then dipping generously into freshly blended Za’atar. It’s still my favorite meal (and now Asad’s 🥰). 

Happy #WorldZaatarDay! Grateful to be from a region of the world rich in flavors and traditions that I get to share with all of you. 

Got to bless the media with these super cute Zeit & Za’atar send-outs from @zaytounpublicity & @paliroots 😋 with olive oil made from the PaliRoots family olive grove in TurmusAyyha, Palestine.

I’ve always been fascinated by Bedouin history. Especially the history of Bedouin women (they are so badass so maybe I’m hoping to find ancestral connections along the way?). 

If there are any haram police still lingering on my profile (I think I’ve done a pretty decent job at weeding them out over the years) - now is a good time to swipe ☺️ 

I absolutely love tattoos. Everything about them from the art used to decorate the body, to the dedication and strength it takes to permanently add something to your being, to the trust you must have in the artist decorating your person. 

Tattoos, particularly on the face, were very prominent in Bedouin culture in pre Islamic era. A woman would choose to tattoo her face for a number of reasons. Everything from the belief that tattoos added spiritual protection and aiding in pain prevention/relief to them being a way to affordably decorate ones body (often referred to a “poor man’s gold) to public displays of faith and identity. In many cultures tattoos symbolize what tribe one belongs to. 

Tattooing of the face is a fading traditional art form in the Middle East and North African regions. 

I’ve been slowly learning more about the Bedouins of Palestine and the ancient practice of facial tattoos as beauty standards of the time, but after seeing @quannah.rose absolutely SLAY at the #MetGala with her absolutely gorgeous tattoos it encouraged me to speed up the learning process. 

I’ve mentioned before that I find a lot of inspiration from the indigenous American community, and especially admire their loyalty to their ancestors and traditions. I cannot thank indigenous influencers enough for giving me the courage to dig deeper and share pieces of Palestinian culture that I never imagined learning about before ❤️🤲🏽 

Note: the woman in the black & white photo is an Amazigh woman from Tinzit, Morocco - Bedouin women from the MENA region shared similar beauty standards.

A day late (purposefully this time because for the first time in 5 or 6 years I let my dad have his birthday to himself 😆) but yesterday was “National Dog Day” (these “holidays” are getting exhausting but the mom guilt is real 🥲) and my pup deserves love. 

There’s a lot of taboo surrounding the concept of owning a dog in the Muslim community. My paternal grandfather (God rest his soul) used to make us run into the house to wash our hands 7 times if he caught us petting a puppy. I don’t fault anyone for that mindset because it’s something passed down each generation as just an accepted belief. But I think my generation may be the last to have been raised to see dogs as “haram”. We were taught to love and respect animals - but to love dogs specifically from a far. 

I’ll admit it was tough at first for my family when I brought Stella home. Literally no one could believe we got a dog. She was so damn cute but the cultural construct (because it is absolutely not religious) around owning a dog in your home was tough to break through at first. 

There are a lot false, and harmful beliefs (that again, aren’t in line with religious scripture) about dogs that are slowly being forgotten/unlearned in the Muslim community. There are 2 mentions of dogs in the Quran. The 1st permitting humans to eat the meat hunted by dogs. The 2nd a sweet story about a child who was protected by a dog as they laid across the entrance to a cave guarding him. That’s it. 

Personally, I live by the belief that God (who is merciful and compassionate) wants all of his creations to be loved and cared for. Stella came from a puppy mill down in Georgia. She was the runt of the litter. Had a piece of her ear missing. Was (and still is) terrified of anything that stands/flies/hovers above her (which is everything). And was definitely in need of love and care (as was I). 

I remember how lucky I am each time I open the front door, and she is wagging her tail excited and grateful that we came home. 

Happy #NationalDogDay to my sweet girl. 🐕 💕

Relief - in knowing that “I’ve got this” and learning that I can trust myself. 

Gratitude - in being able to experience this awakening at what is still a young age. 

Anger - in realizing how strategic our society is in holding women back - particularly women of color - from recognizing and connecting with our power. 

In the last two years I have made massive strides towards becoming the person I am meant to be in this life (I attribute that to motherhood for making me laser-focused on my goals). Alas, another part of that inner growth is recognizing that you can’t take everyone with you on your journey and that that is OK, because making space for new people and new thoughts has led me to connecting with so many amazing humans and experiences that have led me to feeling more connected with my roots and ancestors than ever before. 

Thank you to everyone who has chosen to be a part of my journey. And for anyone going through growing pains right now - I promise it is worth it. Do you know the connection between Palestine & watermelons? It’s more than just a fruit we famously grew in Jenin. It’s a symbol of hope, of freedom, of heritage - of resistance. 

“All that from a fruit?” 

I know it sounds wild - but the story behind it all will make your head spin in awe of Palestinian creativity. 

After The Six-Day War in 1967, the Israeli government passed a law banning any & all public displays of the Palestinian flag along w. its colors (red, white, black, & green) in things like advertisements, photographs, etc. Disobeying this law would result in imprisonment (or a beating, depends on how lucky you were on any given day). Can you imagine being threatened with jail for using a color?

Because of the similarities in colors it became a subtle form of public protest to walk through the streets of the West Bank and Gaza holding slices of watermelon (there are some stories of Palestinians being arrested for this). 

13 years later in 1980, Israel passed another law further suppressing Palestinians freedom of expression, this time through our art - banning the production of any art that “reflected political significance.” (Tying into our story of how #Thobes were turned into symbols of resistance). 

Palestinian artists were forbidden to paint with the colors of the Palestinian flag, leading to a conversation between artist Issam Badr and an IDF soldier during the raid & shut down of an art exhibition because Israel believed the art broke the new law, where he (Badr) asks, “And what if I were to paint a flower of red, green, black, & white?” to which the soldier replies, “Even if you paint a watermelon, it will be confiscated.” 

Because we are a courageously clever & defiant people, watermelon remained even more now our symbol of hope for freedom. 

I hope you’re enjoying a #SliceOfResistance watermelon today! Here’s my own twist on a Palestinian watermelon salad.

There are so many levels to cultural appropriation that people don’t truly understand. Nor do they understand the detrimental impact it has on an entire group of people. When you Google “Israeli street food” a list of foods literally in Arabic come up. 

Hummus - the Arabic word for chickpea. 

Shawarma - the Arabic word for “turning” (which is how the meat is cooked for a shawarma sandwich) 

Falafel - deriving from the Arabic word “filfil” meaning pepper

All Arabic words, rebranded as Israeli. All dishes from the Levant having never been assigned to a single country because pre colonization our part of the world never needed to claim ownership of our cultural practices and pieces. 

There are so many other staple foods, some of which are specifically Palestinian and are not eaten anywhere else, that have been culturally appropriated (I can’t explain the temperature of my blood when grocery shopping and seeing “Israeli couscous” on shelves). When I was 24 I discovered Sufism, and I was FASCINATED. I still consider myself a Sunni Muslim, but Sufism is in my blood. Part 2️⃣: Political Symbolism & Importance 

It wasn’t until the “Arab Revolt” against the British in 1936, that the #keffiyeh became a political symbol of resistance for Palestinians. The keffiyeh was no longer just a practical piece of clothing for weather related needs. It was being used to cover the faces of Palestinian rebels and freedom fighters in an effort to avoid identification which led to arrest. 

Because of this use, the keffiyeh was eventually banned by the British, and the Palestinian response was for ordinary civilians to begin wearing it to make it more difficult for the British to identify rebels from civilians. (We have always found clever ways to protect our people from ALL of our occupiers.) 

The keffiyeh’s political symbolism strengthened greatly during the First #Intifada in 1987, and again in the Second Intifada in 2000.
