Part 1️⃣: The Keffiyeh

You guys chose this one to go first! So here it goes 🥰

The #Keffiyeh (also spelled Kufiyah/Kuffiyah) is the famous black and white checkered piece of cloth you’ll see at pro-Palestine protests and a part of essentially all Palestinian related events and culture today. 

It actually holds a history dating back to the Sumerians and Babylonians in Mesopotamia, where it was worn by high priests and was seen as a symbol of high-rank and honor. 

By the time it made its way to Palestine, it became a staple headcovering adopted by Bedouins and land workers as protection from the sun and sand. It comes in many color variations, but most traditionally are the black and white, and red and white combinations. 

The next two posts will cover how the keffiyeh became a symbol of Palestinian resistance and why it’s important to acknowledge its deep connection to Palestine and why Palestinians are so rightfully angry when it’s appropriated by massive mainstream fashion brands.

Part 2️⃣: Colors. 

Colors on a #Thobe are one of the biggest indicators of what city a woman comes from. 

Thobes in Gaza are made with vibrant red (almost purplish) colors, while Thobes hailing from Hebron are a deep red with hints of brown (where this skirt is most likely from). And Thobes with threads of darker more potent reds are known to come from cities like Bethlehem, Jaffa (pronounced: “Yah-Fah”), and Ramallah. 

Designs and patterns of the embroidery went into even further detail. Orange flowers alongside Cupressus trees are prominent designs on Thobes from Jaffa because those are what surround the village of Beit Dajan. 

As Palestinian land began to shrink and the region became more politically charged, the designs on women’s dresses began to morph to tell different, more intense stories. 

In the 1980s Israel passed a law banning any and all political symbols showing Palestinian pride or nationalism. No flags. No colors of the flag (this is where the story of the watermelon comes in). And anything depicting Palestinian nationality was confiscated (this still happens today). 

Because our women are clever and boss AF (😎), they began replacing the embroidered flowers and cross stitching on their Thobes with embroidered images of the Palestinian flag, the Dome of the Rock, and other symbols of Palestinian pride - because clothing could not be legally confiscated.

I’ve always had severe separation anxiety from my mother. She gives off a very angelic vibe - the energy she puts out is always good and kind (she descends from famous Sufi mystics of the Boukhari line so it makes sense). There is no one on this earth like her and because of that, I felt like in order to “protect” her, I needed to be around her 24/7. 

She enrolled me in gymnastics classes when I was about 6 years old. I made her stay for the full hour of gymnastics in the seating area with a glass window on the second floor, and I would turn around every 5 minutes to make sure she was there or I’d literally cry and throw up (we now know this is how children show signs of anxiety 🙃). 

She stayed the entire class every week, even though most parents would’ve left, with my 2 years old and essentially newborn brothers. To help pass the time and be somewhat productive - she learned how to French braid hair during my gymnastics classes. 

It became something I loved having her do - braiding my hair. She’d braid my hair for all of my sports events, early in the morning before school, every once in a while even now I’ll ask her to braid it for me. It reminds me of when I was little and it makes me feel like I’m still her little girl. 

I never knew how symbolic braids were to indigenous women. After researching it some more I learned yet another connection of indigenous Palestinians to indigenous tribes around the globe - that our hair is sacred. Long hair, particularly in braids, represents a strong cultural identity. It’s considered a sign of resilience and power in both men and women, and is believed to connect us to our ancestors. 

Because @worldviabelal is a thoughtful genius behind the lens, he chose this pose knowing how important it was to me to learn to embrace my hair - not even realizing that it would unintentionally become a recreation of this photo of Bedouin women in Jericho in the 1860s (SWIPE ➡️). 

And so a sweet moment with my mama that brought me back to my childhood, during a photoshoot I scheduled to help me connect with my ancestors, did exactly that.

The Nakba.

The Nakba is the Arabic word for “The Catastrophe”. It refers back to a time in 1948 when Israel declared its statehood by the violent ethnic cleansing of indigenous Palestinians (they celebrate it as “Independence Day” while we mourn). A topic that is legally banned from being taught in Israeli schools. 

The Nakba lead to 750,000+ Palestinians becoming refugees and being expelled from their homes. My grandfather being one of them. As well as Saif’s grandparents who survived a massacre of their native village that claimed the lives of 47 of their family members (they were lined up and shot individually execution style). His grandmother survived because at 8 years old she was “clever enough” to cover her face in her murdered grandmother’s blood and lay next to her body and play dead. 

🔸~Two dozen Palestinian villages were massacred (my husband’s family’s village of Deir Yassin being one of them) 

🔸~400 Palestinian cities and villages were destroyed and/or ethnically cleansed for Jewish repopulation. 

🔸~4.2M acres of Palestinian land stolen. 

That is The Nakba. And it has yet to end.

“Why can’t I just have normal music?” 

All of it stemmed from a place of identity-insecurity. I agreed to 3 Arabic songs. 

***

Fast forward to my wedding in 2017, and there I was once again going back & forth with my mom about the DJ list. Except that this time it was because the music was 85% Arabic and she was worried it’d bore our American friends. 

Our wedding day was my chance to give my friends a real taste of who I am and the culture my family and I love and respect so deeply. It was the first time that many of them saw this side of our family. The “non-American” side.

I couldn’t wait to share this part of me with so many people I loved. It was a celebration of new beginnings and the love between my husband and I, but it was also a celebration of our Palestinian heritage. The one that has survived repeated attempts of genocide. I needed to make sure everyone knew who we were after they left our incredible wedding night. 

There are so many new people who have come to my page over the last few weeks (a solid 2200+ of you!). I know what you’re here for and in an effort to make sure you stick around and stay curious about Palestine and my people, I’m taking the opportunity to reshare some of the best moments of my life with you all that were also celebrations of my ancestors' resilience. 

There is nothing in the world quite as beautiful or as meaningful as Palestinian joy. While many of you are here to learn about our present day struggles, I want to make sure that you are also seeing the beauty and happiness of our people. It’s important to me and to our liberation that you see that part of us, too. 

So - here’s a mashup of our perfect Palestinian- American Muslim wedding. A blend of three cultural traditions that, despite what others may tell you, fit together beautifully.

I’ve been made fun of for my nose my whole life. 

It’s been called a beak. Hooked. I’ve been told I need a nose job. Have been made to feel like it’s an “unfortunate” part of what would otherwise be a pretty face. 

It’s something I used to edit in my photos when I was a teenager (I had a field day with Adobe Photoshop). I’d talk about how I was going to save up for a nose job one day. Or how to strategically miss a fly ball during a softball game one day so that it’d conveniently break and be covered by insurance (I didn’t have the balls for that let’s be honest). 

I always wanted to be the blonde girl with blue eyes and a button nose with a smooth slope. I felt like this for years, and I grew up with parents who told me every day that I was the most beautiful girl in the world and that I was perfect just the way God made me and that nothing needed to change. 

If I could feel this way (sometimes I still do - especially with “liquid nose jobs” popping up all over my Instagram) with all of the love & support I had at home, imagine what these bullshit beauty standards are doing to young girls who don’t get that kind of support at home. 

Stop setting standards for women (and just generally for all humans). Beauty, success, etc. They all have to go.

I am so honored to have been asked by @shehzilm  to collaborate with her on a piece for Palestine. Shehzil asked me to help paint a picture of what I want people to know about Palestine today. I used my art form - words - to help her visualize and curate her own form of art and from those words she created this incredible piece. 

Our people are suffering. They have been for 7 decades. The occupation, the ethnic cleansing, the apartheid, the home expulsions, the bombings. It’s all been happening for so long. While it is our reality, I don’t want that to be the only image of Palestine & Palestinians that people see. 

This recent Palestinian uprising is relying heavily on bravery. Our people in Palestine are brave enough to record what is happening to them. They have shown us the Israeli night raids and home invasions; the settlers stealing our homes; the Israeli police and IDF gassing us and shooting us during prayer at Al Aqsa; the IDF bombing us in Gaza. They are brave enough to film it, relying on us in the diaspora to be brave enough to share it widely and continuously. Together, and for the very first time, we have changed this twisted media game forever.

Palestinians everywhere are feeling strong ancestral ties to one another. These are the same ties that bind all indigenous people throughout history who have been colonized and massacred. I feel this connection every time I choose to speak up and not temper my words. I am a vocal vessel for my Palestinian ancestors who survived genocide - and for those who did not. As our ancestors give me the right language to use on my platform to tell our stories, they give our brothers and sisters in Palestine the physical strength to stand up tall and strong against brutality, to pull our people out of the rubble and to simply live on and keep fighting the oppressors. 

This uprising is about our interconnectedness and ancestral lineage. Our ancestors have come back for our right of return, to free our people, and they’re doing it through all of us. And we won’t stop until we do.

I got a handful of messages from my last video talking about all the foods my fellow Arabs miss from childhood because of dietary changes!

I usually make a “khishneh” version with a GF pan-fried duplicated of shredded phyllo dough (think: the way they make funnel cake but on a flat pan and not into boiling hot oil), but I tried a “na3meh” version using GF corn flakes!

🌽 GF corn flakes (make sure they’re GF! Many use malt flavoring)

🧀 Mozzarella & Ricotta cheese

I signed up yesterday & begged her for help. 
✍🏼
I’d like to have another baby one day - but my mind & body aren’t ready. My pregnancy was “fine” (definitely could’ve been better). My labor & delivery were horrific, and my recovery was even worse. And I know now that it was kinda my fault. I didn’t prepare my body for ANY of that trauma. And I am 100% aware that I am even further away from being prepared for it a second time. 
🤚🏼
She told me to start the day with a postnatal recovery barre class. 1.5 years post-birth and this was the first step I took towards “recovery”. It was 30 min of slow, deep movements in my living room, with a stranger on TV telling me to “be proud” of my body. And in that moment I realized I had never thanked my body for allowing me to create the greatest tiny life 1.5 years ago. And I immediately felt guilty & regretted all of the self-deprecating & body-shaming jokes I had been making about myself. And then I cried. Because it was the first workout I had completed since well before I even found out I was pregnant. I realize now that I don’t just want to look good - I want to be/feel strong. And I think this is how I’ll get there.

She spent weekly nights with me on the couch binge watching @Netflix until 3am, brunches together around Hoboken, she treated me to spa days as I neared the end of pregnancy when she knew I was tired and just needed/wanted to be pampered. She was the only person who never canceled our plans because she knew I “needed this” (and because she knew what hormones would do to me). She checked in on me almost daily. And when Asad was born, she was right there in the waiting room for hours, waiting to hear that I was OK and what he was (#arealgenderreveal). 
💗
She was there the next morning, crying holding my new baby, cracking up holding my hand while I cry-laughed as the lactation consultant tore apart my boob with a metal spoon, there two days later holding up my shirt so I could FaceTime her mom (she’s a nurse) and show her said boobs while I cried, “there’s just no milk!”. There when Asad had his first leaky diaper that went all over my pants and she smeared Purell under my nose so I could get through the diaper change without gagging, there every Thursday after that until the day we moved 45 min away and a global pandemic happened - then she was there on FaceTime. 
💗
Angie, I will never, ever, be able to express my gratitude. And since I’ve become a mom, I just ugly-cry whenever I think about how lucky I am to have you as a best friend and sister. Thank you for everything you’ve done and been there for the last 22 years. Happy last “twenties” birthday - I hope we get to celebrate 100 more together. I love you lots, and I’d literally be a psychopath without you.

If the recent passing of an “invincible human” and his sweet 13 year old legacy hasn’t made you pause, reflect, understand & find gratitude in the fragility of this life - do that now. My heart has been hurting for a sister (who I don’t even know) who lost half of her world in one moment. Everything in this life is temporary, the material things you have & want. The beautiful house you worked hard for, the nice car you spent too much money on, the clothes and shoes that you probably don’t need; those are all temporary (all things I am also guilty of putting too much focus on). Temporary things that bring temporary happiness and temporary validation. They don’t define you in this life and they most certainly will not in the next. What defines you is what you leave behind in others who survive you. The way you make people feel, the good things (or the bad) that you have done for the world, the connections you made. Those are the things that bring  genuine happiness, everlasting love & endless light that will live on after you have passed. Unless you are stressing about a roof over your head tonight, and what you will eat tomorrow - you are privileged in this life. Let these moments of sorrow be a reminder; to #pause, #reflect & find #gratitude for all that you have. I am always grateful, #Alhamdullilah, but these last few days I have been overwhelmed with gratitude for the life we have built & that I get to continue to live another day with those I love most. 💕 #RIPKobe #RIPGigi #findyourgratitude #mambamentality #thislifeistemporary #Mylegacy #AsadSaifKawash  #mashallah

👋🏼Not so cute but super real and long (and at times TMI but when has that stopped me before) post in honor of my past life just 30 days ago: ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
I still can’t believe what my body went through and survived a month ago (and fair warning if you ask for my experience I will tell you the whole truth but only if you ask). ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀ ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
I’m still recovering (no matter how many put together photos I might post). I am still sore, still tired, still 30lbs heavier than my pre-pregnancy weight, still bleeding (yes bleeding) and still “off” some days. I struggled with breastfeeding the first two weeks and felt lost because I thought I should just “know” what to do and I absolutely did not (we got it now thanks to an amazing LC). ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
Some days are fantastic. Some days are shitty. Some days are better than others. Some days I feel like I’ve regressed in my overall recovery. But even on bad days, every next day is better than the day before. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀ ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀ ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
It’s not only a physical recovery, it’s also a mental one - that also comes with a non-negotiable, mandatory mentality shift. My entire existence has changed. I’ve been “mourning” the loss of my old, selfish self - and learning to celebrate the new me who was born at that same moment (10:38PM) in the delivery room when my son entered the world. It’s just as much of a struggle as everything I’m physically enduring (some days that struggle is greater). I’m learning to become who my child needs me to be for their well-being, their happiness, their survival (all while learning who to be for all of those reasons for myself, too). ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
I can 100% say without a doubt, that if Saif wasn’t on paternity leave, there’s no way I’d already be this close to “normal”. Between taking turns for the morning “shifts”, changing many more diapers than I have, keeping a clean home so I can take naps and rest, and everything in between, I owe a majority of my recovery to him being around. This is what I saw with him as my future almost 4 years ago - someone who was in it 110% all the time - and I’m so happy my intuition was spot on with that one 🥰 [CONTINUED 👉🏼]

I didn’t want the stereotypical #maternityshoot of in the woods in a gown with a flower crown looking super sexy. Nothing against them, they’re just not “me” or “us”. I don’t feel like the “goddess” everyone tells you you should feel like. I almost feel like I’m having an out of body experience. This pregnancy has been one of the most interesting experiences of my life thus far. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀ ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀ ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀
It’s been a physical journey for my body that changes its course every day. I don’t totally love the way I look but I love my body for what it’s doing and I am grateful for its strength to be able to adapt to all of these changes and provide a safe place for our baby until it’s time they come earth-side. I don’t feel “sexy” but I don’t feel not sexy, either. Some days I feel beautiful, some days I don’t. Some days I feel extra heavy, some days I feel like I could run a marathon. Some days my skin is glowing. Others it looks like I rubbed my face in pizza.🍕Lately I’ve been fluctuating between feeling like superwoman and feeling like a 97-year-old lady as I near the end of this. ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀ ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀ ⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀⠀

It took me a while to really grasp mentally that I was/am pregnant - because I was almost “too educated” on all of the outcomes of pregnancy. Like my brain was protecting me incase my body wasn’t ready for this or decided it wasn’t my time.

⠀

⠀
Today I, along with millions of other women like me, get to see myself and my beloved culture being positively represented in American politics. ⠀
⠀
Representation matters. ⠀
⠀
Regardless of gender, our child will grow up in the America that my parents and grandparents (and my in laws and husband) dreamed of. One that equally represents all of her citizens and makes sure that we make space for all Americans. One that represents his/her ancestry that is being actively erased with help by the very nation that is about to acknowledge our existence in a political ceremony that is so wonderfully ironic to all who know our history and current struggle. To my fellow Palis and Muslim ladies, there is undoubtedly a place for you - for us - in this country. ⠀
⠀
Today – proudly share your beautiful photos of you in your beautiful thobes using the hashtag #tweetyourthobe – and enjoy this even more beautiful moment in our country’s history. We belong here.⠀
⠀

They are were the only books I'd voluntarily read - mainly because they were all real stories, many of which I could personally connect with. They are what sparked my interest in story telling - and it's how I learned that opening up about something you are struggling with - could help a stranger somewhere in the world. 
We're starting 2018 off with an incredibly big step forward. Today, we've officially announced/released our 1st of many editions (inshallah) of the "MissMuslim Memoirs"! A print version of all of our favorite and most read pieces of 2017. Stories that have helped people through personal struggles, and that have promoted self-acceptance and tolerance for what others may be experiencing. 
It's our "Chicken Soup for the Soul" - #MM style! ;) I couldn't be prouder of our team! Every story in this book was written by an incredible woman - most of these authors being minority women - with an incredible story. This book is a product of 365+ days of passion and dedication to our platform and to our message. It would not exist (nor would our amazing site) without them. 
The best part about buying a copy of this book: part of the proceeds will be going to the Girls Not Brides organization in an effort to end child marriages and help girls reach their full potential. 
Had you told me in 2017 that we'd be a team of published authors - I'm not sure I'd have believed you. But life seems to be pleasantly surprising me by the hour. Congratulations to all of our writers! 
So - without further ado - I'd like to introduce you all to the "#MissMuslimMemoirs: 2017"! 💋

In 1927, @natgeo printed a special edition highlighting the historical beauty and religious diversity of #Palestine, specifically Jerusalem - which I am lucky to own a copy of. The first man you’ll see in this album, is my great great grandfather, head of the Sufi #Naqshabandi order in Palestine at the time, Sheikh Yacoub Boukhari (one of 27 #autochromed photos - the rest of the book is black & white). May he Rest In Peace. Pictured next is the Christian Armenian Patriarch (which runs  and protects the Holy Sepluchre today), a Hungarian and Yemenite Jew in traditional clothing reading from their Holy text, the Egyptian Coptic Bishop at the time, and the Greek Orthodox Patriarch dressed in Easter clothing. Today was a sad day to be Palestinian and as I contemplated what to post - the only thing that is repeated in my mind is this: since its very beginning, #Jerusalem has been holy ground for all three Abrahamic faiths. It has been a place of knowledge and understanding. A place where history lives on through all of those who pray within its walls. A place of holiness and reflection for all pious people. But most importantly it has been a place of neutrality for everyone. And that is how it should remain. Jerusalem is the key to peace and war. We should choose peace, every time. #HandsOffJerusalem

Day 4: We are spent. All the love and admiration for the doctors and nurses and teachers and rescuers and other volunteers who do this for months at a time. Saif did amazing as per usual. Though I think he's having some trouble switching back to English now 🤦🏻‍♀️. I think the count was around 80 patients today. I was able to help out a bit more this time! And there were tons of kids to play with. I taught my new 4 year old friend how to play tic-tac-toe on a piece of gauze and his response after 3 games was "shoo hiloo!" (so nice!). I bonded with the sweetest pup (don't tell Stella!🐾) who the Kurdish children call "Max" and the Arab children call "Ahoueh" (coffee 😂 he is a bit coffee colored). I got to use my tiny vocabulary of Arabic to play with everyone. The last two days definitely left a lifelong impression on @saifyk and I. Of course, there will be a post soon, but in the meantime, please - if you speak another language (majority spoke Arabic, French, Kurdish and Farsi), have a medical background, or just have a desire to help other people however you can - please consider volunteering if not with #ERCI then with another organization. It is as rewarding in spirit for oneself as it is for those who are in need of your empathy. We will definitely be doing this again very soon. Thanks again to Emergency Response Centre International for allowing us to take part in this experience. Tomorrow - the relaxing honeymoon that everyone talks about can finally begin. Day 3! @saifyk and I took a detour to #Lesvos for two days to volunteer with Emergency Response Centre International in their clinic in the Moria refugee camp (thanks to @dnpali7 on our team at @missmuslimnyc for connecting us with this amazing organization). I stood back in awe and was filled with an overwhelming sense of pride as I watched my husband translate for over 30+ patients who only spoke #Arabic and were seeking various medical treatments (I was useless in the translation department so I mopped floors and held hands 🙃). I had no expectations or assumptions of the next two days - we had no idea what we were about to get into when joining this incredible team of medics and translators and field coordinators. These doctors and nurses and volunteers and refugees are some of the strongest, most resilient people I've ever met in my life. Today reminded me (not that I need a reminder) that I married the most remarkable man. I fought back tears all day while watching him work with children of just 2 years old to elders of around age 70+. I am so honored to be his wife. After a nearly 12 hour straight shift, we caught a beautiful sunset at the harbor of the city. One more day of volunteering and then it's off to the next island for the Kawash's! After the most amazing week of my/our life, I decided to burn some bakhoor for the first time for a little added protection and blessings☺️🙏🏼. #Bakhoor (this one is benzoin resin) was first largely promoted around the Middle East and afterward in the vast territory of the Muslim world. It is believed to help one's mood in order to bring peaceful, tranquil, refreshing, uplifting & inspiring feelings. It opens the mind to spirituality & diverts from worldly impurities. It is said to dispel malicious and distressing psychic forces and improve memory while being burned and simultaneous playing Quran. It is used in multiple faiths as a way to "clear the air" of negativity and make room for prayers and good vibes. I used a brass burner, placed burning charcoal on the top cage and then placed a small piece of bakhoor above it. Major thanks to @jmansy for walking me through the steps! I will be doing this more often. 🌙📿 #Islam #Sufism #ilovemyreligion

Since this day 69 years ago - 7 million Palestinians lost the right to return home. My grandfather is one of those 7 million - and one of the first 700,000 who were expelled from their homes on this day in 1948. I am the product of refugees - so is my future husband. Despite the attempts of many to erase us and our history - we will always exist no matter where that may be in the world. This was my grandfather's home (which no longer exists) of Ein Karem - a predominantly Christian city where it is believed that #JohnTheBaptist was born. My family was one of few Muslim families living in the city in a time where religious harmony and acceptance was once the norm. He tells me stories of his Christian neighbors, his Jewish butcher and better - more peaceful times - that he still hopes will be our reality once again. #ThisIsMyHistory #NakbaDay #ProudPalestinian ✊🏼🇵🇸

A year ago I gave myself the greatest birthday gift imaginable - a community and online home for women who have gone through life feeling alone or struggling to figure out where they belonged - to now have a place where they feel empowered, included, supported and *safe* to share their stories of triumph over struggle and to demolish the stereotypes and taboos that are used in attempt to confine and control us. 
The past year with MissMuslim has been like a dream where some days I can't believe how quickly we have achieved so much greatness and thinking about what is yet to come excites and terrifies me! Our site is proof that if the right intentions are behind a project - the Universe will allow it to flourish naturally and with ease. 
Every girl has a fairy tale story of her own that she dreams of but is not always sure will be reached - our #MM family is my fairy tale come true and it's been even better than I could have imagined.

Thank you to every single editor, writer, reader, family member, friend, Instagram "liker", Facebook acquaintance and every outlet that has helped amplify our voices. None of this would be possible without your stories, your readership, your passion, your values, your truths, your support. 
I have never been more proud of anything in my life. 
Thank you everyone who has been reaching out with wonderfully thoughtful birthday messages! I am honored to read your words. 
Happy 1st birthday/1 year anniversary to #MissMuslim, happy 26th birthday to my Teddi Buttons (my teddy bear) - and happy first day of Women's History Month to all the badass women in my life and those around the world fighting for equality and freedom and dignity. This is our year - I can feel it. 💋

Today is Eid Al-Adha! 
Also referred to as "The Feast of Sacrifice" (or the Big Eid when you were growing up a Muslim kid in America) is one of the holiest days on the Islamic calendar. 
Today, Muslims all over the world are celebrating prophet Abraham (PBUH) and his willingness to sacrifice his son upon God's request as an act of submission. As God recognized Abraham's devotion, He intervened through the Angel Gabriel and instead requested that Abraham sacrifice a lamb. 
As part of tradition, Muslims sacrifice a lamb on Eid Al-Adha. The lamb is supposed to be cut into three parts - 1/3 for the family performing the sacrifice, 1/3 is given to relatives and the remaining third is given to the poor. Today, most families typically have a whole lamb for themselves and their relatives for a party and donate another lamb to the poor (usually overseas). Today I get to wear my fancy new traditional Palestinian thobe - from Palestine! 
#EidMubarak to everyone celebrating today! 
May your lives always be blessed with love and family, may your hearts always be filled with happiness and compassion and may your prayers always be heard and answered. 💚🙏🏻🎉

14 years ago today the life of every American citizen drastically changed. White, Black, Latino, Muslim, Christian, Jew. For one day there were no labels - we were all simply, American. 
On this day, over 3,000 American children lost a parent. 
I will never forget being the first child pulled out of school on this day, and my parents doing the best they could to explain to a 5th grader, a 2nd grader and a kindergartener that this was what evil looked like and what it was capable of. 
At 10 years old, I had absolutely no idea how much this day would influence my life as a Muslim American. 
I hope that one day soon we can be unified again - not just in tragedy. 
May the victims of this day, American - and everywhere else in the world - rest in peace.
